title: Our Mutual Friend: A Literary Discussion

segments.title: Opening: The Dust Heaps and the City of Souls

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked — a close, passionate, sometimes argumentative journey through what many consider Dickens's last great completed novel.
I'm your host, and today we begin at the very beginning — with a river that carries a corpse, a fortune built on dust, and a city that seems to feed on its own dead.

Our Mutual Friend was published in 1864 and 1865, the last novel Dickens completed before his death — and there's something in it that feels like a great writer settling every account he ever had with the world.
To help us unpack it, I've brought together three people whose minds I trust completely with a book this rich.
Oliver Trevelyan has lent his voice to more classic novels than almost anyone alive — he hears Dickens the way a musician hears a score, rhythms and rests and all.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don whose faith in the moral imagination of great fiction is, frankly, a corrective the rest of us need.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has been re-reading this novel since she was a teenager, and brings to it something rarer than scholarship — genuine love.
Let's begin where the novel begins — on the Thames, in the dark, with Gaffer Hexam and his daughter Lizzie, dragging the river for what Gaffer calls, with magnificent matter-of-factness, his living.
What strikes me every single time I return to that opening — and I've read it aloud more times than I can count — is how completely Dickens trusts the scene to speak for itself.
No preamble, no throat-clearing — you're in the boat, on the river, at night, and this grim old man is pulling something toward you.
And then Dickens gives us one of the great opening sentences in all of English fiction.
"In these times of ours, though concerning the exact year there is no need to be precise, a boat of dirty and disreputable appearance, with two figures in it, floated on the Thames."
"Floated" — not rowed, not moved — floated.
There's a passivity in that word — as if the river itself is in charge — that sets the entire moral atmosphere of the book.
Dickens is telling you, from the very first sentence: in this world, things drift.
Oliver is quite right about the craft, though I'd locate its achievement slightly differently.
What Dickens establishes in those first pages is not an atmosphere of capitalism, as certain critics would have it — it is an atmosphere of moral emergency.
Gaffer Hexam is a man who has decided that the dead have no claims on the living — that a drowned man's pocket is fair salvage.
That is not a critique of an economic system — that is a portrait of a particular moral deformity.
And Dickens is scrupulous about it: he gives Gaffer a kind of inverted pride — the man won't rob the living, only the dead.
It's a distinction Gaffer holds to with genuine dignity, which is precisely what makes him so disturbing.
What I find I can't get past — and I mean this as the highest compliment — is Lizzie.
She's in the boat with her father, she's doing this work — pulling dead men from the river — and she never flinches.
But Dickens is very careful to show us that she is ashamed of it.
There's this image that comes back throughout the early chapters — Lizzie looking into the fire and seeing pictures there.
She reads the fire the way other people read books, because she can't read books — her father won't allow it.
And yet she dreams of something better for Charley, her brother — she's saving him from the river even as she sits in the boat.
That tension — between loyalty to the world she comes from and longing for something she can barely name — that is the emotional engine of this entire novel.
And then, almost in the same breath, Dickens introduces us to the other world — the Veneerings.
If the Thames opening is one of the great dark entrances in English fiction, the Veneering dinner table is one of the great comic ones.
Dickens tells us that everything about the Veneerings is new — the house is new, the furniture is new, the plate is new, the carriage is new, the harness is new.

"All their furniture was new, all their friends were new, all their servants were new, their plate was new, their carriage was new, their harness was new, their horses were new, they themselves were new."
The joke is unstoppable — the repetition is like a hammer, but a comic hammer.
And the final twist — "they themselves were new" — that's the sting at the end.
These people have manufactured themselves out of nothing, and Dickens is telling you that's exactly as absurd as it sounds.
The Veneerings are a satire on social newness, certainly — but I think one must be careful not to read the novel as simply an attack on the nouveaux riches.
Dickens is too honest for that.
The old aristocracy — represented by the Podsnaps and their circle — is no better.
Podsnap, with his magnificent certainty that England is the greatest country on earth and that anything foreign is simply not done — Podsnap is the old world's version of the Veneerings.
Both are hollow.
Dickens's target is not a class — it's a moral condition: the substitution of appearance for substance at every level of society.
And the dust heaps hold both worlds together — that's what I keep coming back to.
Old Harmon's fortune is built on the heaps — on rubbish, on what London throws away.
And Dickens understood something profound about that: in this society, what is discarded becomes wealth.
The dust is money, money is dust — and the whole novel turns on who inherits that ambiguity.
Young John Harmon — or the man we think is John Harmon — comes back to claim a fortune he never wanted, from a father he feared.
And the only way he can survive that world with his soul intact is to disappear into it.
Disappear into it — and what a disappearance that is.
Identity — its loss, its construction, its recovery — is the great subject of this novel.
We have a drowned man who isn't drowned, a villain who poses as a friend, a miser's fortune that transforms everyone it touches.
In a moment, we'll look more closely at the world Dickens builds around that fortune — the people who want it, the people it destroys, and the few rare souls who want nothing to do with it.

segments.title: The Comedy of Names and the Grotesque

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
We are deep in a novel that is, among many other things, one of the great comic achievements in the English language.
And nowhere is that comedy more extravagant — or more precise — than in the names Dickens gives his characters.
This segment we are turning to the grotesque: the comedy of nomenclature, the exuberance of caricature, and the strange way Dickens makes the ridiculous feel absolutely real.
Oliver Trevelyan — you are the man who has read more Dickens aloud than perhaps anyone living.
Where do we begin with the names in this novel?
Where do we begin? You could spend an entire afternoon just reading the cast list aloud and it would constitute a performance.
Silas Wegg. Mr Venus. Noddy Boffin. The Lammles. Rogue Riderhood.
These are not names in any naturalistic sense. They are declarations. They announce their owners before the characters have said a word.
Silas Wegg is the one I adore most as a performer. That name is practically a sentence.
There is something withered and wooden in those two syllables — Wegg — long before you discover that the man has a wooden leg and sells ballads from a street stall.

And then Dickens introduces him as a man who had somehow impaled himself on a ballad-stall — which is exactly the right image for a man whose entire existence is a kind of awkward, opportunistic perch.
The name and the image belong together. That is Dickensian comedy at its most precise.
What strikes me about the names in this novel is how they carry the comedy in the very sound of them, even before meaning enters.
Mr Venus. Just say it. There is something both ridiculous and rather melancholy in that name.
The goddess of love — and here is a man who articulates human skeletons for a living, who is lovesick and lives among anatomical specimens in a shop so cluttered it barely admits the light.
Dickens gives him this wonderful line where he describes his own trade with a kind of mournful pride.
He says — and I am not inventing this — "I'm in the bones."
Three words, and they contain an entire life.
He is in the bones professionally and — Dickens implies — existentially.
The grotesque here is not cruel. It is — strangely — tender.
I am glad Caroline has introduced that word — tender. Because I think too often the grotesque in Dickens is discussed as if it were merely satirical machinery.
But in Our Mutual Friend, the grotesque is, I would argue, a mode of moral vision.
Take Mr and Mrs Veneering. Those names are not incidental. They diagnose a civilisation.
Dickens tells us that everything about them is new — their house, their furniture, their friends, their plate, their carriage.
The name Veneering is itself the novel's central argument about the nouveaux riches — surface without substance, shine without depth.
Now, I resist the temptation to read this as a political treatise on capitalism. Dickens is not writing a pamphlet.
He is observing, with the novelist's unfailing moral instinct, what happens to human character when identity becomes performance.
And the comedy of the Veneerings — their interminable dinner parties, their manufactured intimacies — is funny precisely because it is true.
Edmund is right about the Veneerings, and I want to add: the mirror. That magnificent mirror.

Dickens describes the great looking-glass above the Veneering sideboard as reflecting everything at their dinner table — the guests, the silver, the host and hostess — as if it were a piece of the furniture itself.
It is one of the novel's great comic conceits: a world so vain it exists primarily as its own reflection.
And then Dickens introduces us to Twemlow, that dear bewildered gentleman, perpetually uncertain whether he is the Veneerings' oldest or newest friend.
Twemlow! That name. It is both vaguely aristocratic and faintly absurd — which is exactly what the man is.
Dickens describes him as a piece of living-room furniture — a harmless piece of old china in a new house.
The genius is that by the very end of the novel, that piece of old china turns out to have more moral backbone than anyone else in the room.
Twemlow's moment at the end — his little speech at the last Veneering dinner — is one I find genuinely moving.
All through the novel he has been gently comic — muddled, mild, used. And then he stands up for Wrayburn's marriage to Lizzie Hexam.
He says — and I love this — that a gentleman who married for love and was not ashamed of it did what a gentleman ought to do.
"That the young woman was a lady in the truest sense of the word" — Twemlow says something like this, quietly, against the whole assembled company.
And then he goes home. No fanfare. He simply goes home.
The comedy of Twemlow's name and position makes that moment of quiet courage all the more devastating.
That is what Dickens's grotesque does at its best: it earns the emotion by first making you laugh.
One name in this novel I confess I find almost too perfectly constructed to be entirely natural is Rogue Riderhood.
The man carries the word Rogue as a Christian name — as if his own parents had inscribed his moral character on his birth certificate.
And Riderhood — riding the hood of the river, lurking at the margin between the living world and the dead water.
What is remarkable is that Dickens grants this man — this informer, this blackmailer, this thorough scoundrel — a scene of extraordinary power when he nearly drowns and is brought back to life.
The watchers around him notice that as consciousness returns, the Rogue comes back too — that the kindness glimpsed in unconsciousness retreats as the eyes open.
It is a grotesque scene, but it is also, I would argue, a scene of genuine moral seriousness about the nature of character.
Can a name be a destiny? Dickens seems to ask that question — and to answer it, rather bleakly, yes.
Edmund has touched on something that I find absolutely thrilling as a performer — the question of whether the grotesque name imprisons or liberates.
Because look at Noddy Boffin. The Golden Dustman. There is a name that should announce a buffoon — and yet Boffin is one of the most humane presences in the entire novel.
Dickens gives him this habit of referring to himself in the third person — Boffin says "Boffin's Bower" as if he were both the character and the audience watching him.
And the scene where he appears to become a miser — reading aloud the histories of famous misers with increasing relish — is one of the great sustained performances in the comic novel.
When the truth is revealed — that it was all a stratagem to protect John Harmon and test Bella — it is funny and touching in almost equal measure.
The grotesque exterior — the ridiculous name, the dustheaps, the comic manner — conceals a moral intelligence that puts the supposedly respectable characters to shame.
What I hear in all of this is a novelist who understands that comedy is not the opposite of seriousness — it is its vehicle.
The names are comic, the manners are comic, the situations can be wildly, deliciously absurd — and yet the moral weight never slips.
When we return, we will be looking at the river — its darkness, its secrets, and the strange community that lives and dies along its banks.
Stay with us.

segments.title: Bella's Currency: From Mercenary to Moral Being

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
We turn now to one of the novel's most fully realised characters: Bella Wilfer.
She begins the story as a declared mercenary — someone who has announced, with considerable candour, that she intends to marry for money.
And yet by the novel's end she has undergone what might be called a complete moral currency exchange.
Oliver, you've voiced Bella in the audiobook — you've lived inside her sentences.
What is Dickens doing with her from the very first pages?
The remarkable thing about Bella is that Dickens gives her the bad lines first — and they are genuinely bad lines, in the moral sense.
She sits in that cramped little Wilfer house in Holloway and she tells her father, quite plainly, that she is determined to be rich.
And Dickens doesn't soften it.
He lets her say something to the effect that money is the article she is after, and she won't pretend otherwise.
Now, as a performer, you instinctively ask: is this vanity, is this wit, or is this genuine cupidity?
And Dickens's masterstroke is that it's all three simultaneously — which is why she's so alive on the page.
She has been left a legacy by a dead stranger — old Harmon — and she resents it bitterly, because it has made her feel like a piece of property herself.
So the mercenary declaration is also, in a twisted way, a bid for agency.
That idea of property is crucial and I think Dickens plants it with enormous care.
Bella has been bequeathed like a piece of furniture — left to a man she'd never met, by a man she'd never met.
And there's a moment — I always stop at this moment — when she tells Rokesmith that she is the most mercenary little wretch that ever lived.
She says it with something between defiance and self-disgust, and both emotions are completely true.
What Dickens is tracking — very quietly, over hundreds of pages — is the gap between what Bella says she wants and what she actually hungers for.
She wants to be loved for who she is, not traded for who she might become.
I would want to place the emphasis somewhat differently.
Bella's trajectory is not primarily a social argument about women as property.
It is a study in moral education in the classical sense — the education of the will.
Dickens gives Bella every temptation that the age can provide: she is brought into the Boffin household, shown what wealth looks and feels like.
And she is not unmoved by it.
The great test of character in fiction — as Dr. Johnson understood perfectly — is not whether one is tempted, but whether one ultimately chooses rightly.
Bella does choose rightly, and she does so in full knowledge of what she is relinquishing.
Edmund is right about the test, and it's Boffin who administers it — in one of the most theatrically daring passages in the whole novel.
Noddy Boffin — lovable, bear-like Noddy Boffin — appears to undergo a hideous transformation into a miser.
He begins collecting biographies of famous misers.
He becomes cruel to Rokesmith, dismissive of the poor, obsessed with accumulation.
And Bella watches this — and it repels her.
That's the genius of the theatrical construction.
Dickens shows Bella what money actually does to a soul — even a performance of what it does — and she recoils instinctively.
And what moves me about that sequence is that Bella doesn't recoil in a grand rhetorical speech.
She recoils quietly, internally — and then she acts.
She leaves the Boffin household voluntarily, goes back to the Wilfer poverty she had despised.
And then she marries Rokesmith — who she believes is a penniless secretary — for love.
Dickens is quite precise about the conditions.
She must choose poverty knowingly, with open eyes — because only then has she genuinely become a different person.
There is a scene with her father — Pa, as she calls him — that I find extraordinarily tender.
Bella and Rumty Wilfer go to Greenwich together for a little dinner, just the two of them.
And in that scene Dickens allows Bella a kind of grace — a warmth toward someone she loves without complication.
It is the counterweight to all her mercenary declarations.
She is capable of wholly disinterested love — she merely needed circumstances to reveal it.
The Greenwich dinner is delicious — one of the warmest passages in the novel.
Bella treats her father with a kind of mock ceremonious respect — calling him a fairy godfather, planning the menu with enormous seriousness.
And the comedy is suffused with genuine feeling.
Dickens knows — and this is the performer's instinct — that you reveal character in the small, unguarded moments far more than in the great crises.
Bella with her father is Bella without armour.
I want to come back to the moment she confronts Boffin — when she defends Rokesmith.
Because that is the pivot of the whole arc.
Boffin has been publicly humiliating Rokesmith — dismissing him with contempt — and Bella steps forward.
She knows what it costs her materially.
She steps in front of a man she loves and says, essentially: I will not watch this.
That is the moment the transformation becomes irreversible.
And there is something Dickens does afterwards that is not always sufficiently appreciated.
He does not immediately reward Bella for her moral courage.
She goes back to Holloway — to the diminished life — and she makes the best of it with a cheerfulness that is quite moving.
She tries to be a good housekeeper, a good wife, though she is rather comically inept at it.
That ineptitude is itself significant.
She is not a saint; she is a young woman learning, imperfectly, to live by a better set of values.
The domestic comedy is priceless.
Bella attempting cookery, burning things, confessing disasters to Rokesmith with enormous charm.
Dickens is making a very precise point through the comedy.
The elaborate Boffin establishment required no effort from Bella — it was all done for her.
In the small house she has to actually work — to contribute — and the struggle is part of the transformation.
And then there is the revelation — Rokesmith turns out to be John Harmon himself, the heir.
And Bella has already made her choice.
Caroline, does the novel's ending vindicate Bella fully — or is there a degree of having-it-both-ways?
There is absolutely a degree of having-it-both-ways — and I don't think Dickens was unaware of it.
Bella gets virtue and wealth — she chooses right, and is rewarded with everything she originally wanted.
The most honest reading is that the wealth is beside the point — what matters is that she chose not knowing she'd get it.
The choice in ignorance is everything.
I would put it rather more firmly than that.
The structure of the novel requires the reward.
Dickens is writing in a tradition that understands Providence as ultimately just.
To reward Bella materially is not a sentimental compromise — it is the proper completion of the moral argument.
What I love is that Dickens gives Bella her child before he gives her the money.
The baby — the little one she calls the Inexhaustible — arrives while they are still poor.
And Bella is transformed by maternity in a way that feels completely unforced and real.
The wealth, when it arrives, is almost an afterthought — the important things have already happened.
That's a beautiful place to rest for a moment — Bella's real inheritance isn't Harmon money at all.
It's the self she discovered by choosing against it.
We'll be back shortly to look at the novel's great theme of money corrupting — and in some cases, purifying — the men who handle it.

segments.title: The Masked Man: Harmon's Double Life and Narrative Deception

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
We've been circling the dust mounds, the river, the glittering Veneerings — but now we come to the novel's most audacious structural gamble.
John Harmon — or Julius Handford, or John Rokesmith — a man who spends most of this long novel hiding his own identity from every person around him.
With me to unpick this remarkable deception are Oliver Trevelyan, Edmund Leigh, and Caroline Woodcourt.
Oliver — as a performer, you've read this novel aloud more times than most people have read it silently. Where does Harmon's double life sit in the architecture of the whole?
Right at the centre — and slightly to the side of the centre, which is exactly the problem Dickens sets himself and then has to solve.
John Harmon is nominally the hero of this novel, the man whose inheritance drives the entire plot.
And yet for book after book he skulks about Holloway in a secretary's waistcoat, saying very little, watching everything.
There's a magnificent chapter — almost a Dickens soliloquy — where Harmon sits alone and tries to reconstruct what actually happened to him the night of the murder attempt.
He literally cannot trust his own memory. He says something like — he must think it out, stand outside himself and reason about this person who is and is not himself.
It's the most vertiginous piece of first-person reasoning Dickens ever wrote, and it's buried in the middle of Book Two.
I think one has to be honest about the structural cost of this device, before one can admire its ingenuity.
Harmon's concealment requires the reader to accept a sustained improbability — that a man of honour, genuinely in love with Bella Wilfer, will deceive her for the better part of a year.
Dickens asks us to believe the deception is an act of moral testing — he wants to see whether Bella will outgrow her mercenary ambitions without the lure of his money.
That is a defensible motive in the abstract. Whether it is a motive becoming to a gentleman is quite another question.
Johnson would have something tart to say about the man who arranges a wife as one arranges a moral experiment.
Edmund's critique is fair, and I think Dickens half-knows it — which is why he makes Harmon so uncomfortable in his own disguise.
The chapter Oliver mentioned — in Book Two, Chapter Thirteen — is one of the strangest things in Victorian fiction.
Harmon speaks of himself in the third person, as if the John Harmon who lived and the John Rokesmith who exists now are genuinely separate people.
He says something very close to: 'I, a living man, buried the dead man who bore my name.'
'I, a living man, buried the dead man who bore my name.'
That sentence reverses everything — the living man is performing death, and the dead man is acquiring more and more reality as the novel goes on.
And when you read it aloud, that third-person construction does something uncanny to the voice.
You can't settle on a tone. Is he grieving for himself? Is he relieved? Is there a dark private comedy in it?
When I perform that chapter, I play it on a kind of suspended breath — as if the character himself doesn't know which emotion to land on.
Which is, I think, precisely what Dickens intended — a man genuinely estranged from his own name and story.
The estrangement is real — but I would locate its source not in existential unease but in a very specific inheritance of bad fathering.
Old Harmon treated his son as a piece of property to be disposed of — the fortune conditional on marrying a woman the son had never met.
John Harmon's impersonation is in some sense the son's revenge on his father's will — he refuses to simply walk into the role assigned to him.
That is perfectly coherent moral psychology, whatever one thinks of the mechanics.
That's exactly where I find myself moved by Harmon — not by the disguise itself but by what it costs him emotionally.
He is watching Bella Wilfer day after day — watching her change, soften, discover her own better nature — and he cannot tell her who he is.
There's an almost unbearable tenderness in those scenes at Wilfer's house where he sits at the dinner table as the secretary, the invisible man.
Dickens understands — acutely — the particular loneliness of being loved for a name that isn't yours.
And of course that tension feeds directly into the novel's wider obsession with false identities — Boffin pretending to become a miser, Bella pretending not to love Rokesmith.
Oliver — is there a moment where the disguise nearly cracks? Where Harmon almost gives himself away?
Several moments — but the richest is when Bella, in a burst of wounded pride, tells Rokesmith she will not be proposed to by a secretary.
And Harmon — as Rokesmith — simply absorbs it. Stands there and takes the humiliation.
He cannot defend himself without revealing everything. So he wears her contempt like a second disguise, layered on top of the first.
It's a brilliantly theatrical construction — the man who cannot speak his own name enduring insult in silence.
It is also, if we are being precise, where the novel's narrative deception becomes a deception practised on the reader as well as the characters.
Dickens withholds Harmon's interior life from us for much of the early going — we see him from outside, as Julius Handford at the inquest, as the quiet lodger.
The chapter of self-examination comes almost as a corrective — Dickens suddenly grants us access and then retreats again.
It is a curiously modern technique for a novelist of his generation — the unreliable narrative surface that conceals a reliable interior.
What moves me most is the moment of revelation — when Harmon finally tells Bella the truth, and she has already proven, beyond any doubt, that she loves John Rokesmith.
She married him in poverty, walked away from the Boffin fortune, chose love over money with absolute clarity.
And then the man she loves turns out to be wealthy after all — which is a kind of fairy tale, but an emotionally earned one.
The disguise has done its work. The test was cruel, but the result is Bella transformed — genuinely transformed, not merely forgiven.
And Dickens rewards Bella handsomely — the little boy at the end, the cottage, the genuine happiness.
But what I always come back to is the name. The novel is called Our Mutual Friend — and that phrase belongs to Boffin, not to Harmon.
Harmon is the mutual friend — the connecting tissue of the whole story — and yet he is the person most people in the novel believe is dead.
The absent centre. The title character who has no title, no name, and for most of the novel, no face.
The absent centre — that's a phrase I suspect we'll return to.
Thank you all — Harmon's double life turns out to be a kind of mirror for every other false performance in this most theatrical of novels.
We'll be back after the break to look at those other performances — the Boffin deception, the Veneering facade, and the question of who in this novel is truly who they claim to be.

segments.title: Reading the Rhythms: Dickens as Entertainer and Moralist

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked — the programme that takes Dickens's last completed novel apart, piece by piece, to see how it works.
Our Mutual Friend is a novel of astonishing range — comic grotesquery, moral seriousness, and a Thames running through it like a dark vein.
Today's segment asks a question that cuts to the heart of what Dickens was doing: how does he hold the entertainer and the moralist in the same hand?
Joining me are three guests who've lived with this novel and thought hard about it.
Oliver Trevelyan is an actor and writer whose audiobook readings of Dickens have introduced the novels to a new generation — and who hears the prose the way a musician hears a score.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don whose belief in moral imagination over social programme has shaped some of the finest Dickens criticism of the last fifty years.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read this novel as a teenager and has been arguing about it with herself ever since.
Oliver — let's begin with you, because this is your territory: Dickens the performer.
The first thing I want to say is that Our Mutual Friend is written for the voice — not the eye.
You can read it on the page and admire it, but when you speak it aloud, something clicks into place that simply wasn't there before.
Think of Silas Wegg — this gloriously rotten wooden-legged ballad-monger whom Boffin engages to read to him.
Dickens gives Wegg a voice full of self-satisfied grease — every sentence slipping forward on its own pomposity.
There's a moment when Wegg addresses Boffin as 'a man of an open and generous nature' — and you hear the con in every syllable.
The comedy is entirely in the rhythm — the way Wegg inflates himself while pretending to praise someone else.
That is the entertainer at full stretch — and the moralist is doing the same work at the same moment, showing us exactly what flattery looks like from the inside.
Oliver is right about the voice — I won't dispute that.
But I would resist the implication that the entertainment and the moral seriousness are somehow the same operation.
The greatness of Our Mutual Friend, for me, lies in what Dickens does with character under pressure.
Consider Boffin himself — the Golden Dustman.
There is a sustained act of moral imagination in that figure which goes far beyond comic grotesquery.
Boffin feigns avarice, feigns the corruption that wealth brings — not for his own comfort, but to protect and test John Rokesmith.
That is not satire, strictly speaking — it is a story about goodness disguising itself because goodness, naked, has no power in a corrupt world.
Dickens the moralist is working at a depth the entertainer alone could never reach.
What strikes me, listening to both of you, is that you've each gone to a man — Wegg, Boffin.
And I want to bring in Bella Wilfer, because she is where Dickens's entertainment and moral seriousness are most vulnerably in tension.
Bella is introduced to us as openly, cheerfully mercenary — she wants money, she says so, she makes no apology.
And Dickens writes that confession with such warmth and comic energy that we love her for saying it.
But then comes the moral education — the long, slow arc of her learning what she actually values.
There's a passage — I keep coming back to it — where she says she has been 'too mercenary' and that she despises herself for it.
The rhythm of that self-reproach is completely different from the early comic Bella — it's slower, more internal, more earned.
That shift in rhythm is Dickens signalling the moral shift — the entertainer and the moralist sharing the same instrument.
Caroline puts her finger on exactly the right thing — the rhythm changes.
And when I'm recording these novels, that's the signal I listen for — the moment the prose drops its pace and starts doing something private.
Eugene Wrayburn is another case — one of the most interesting voices in the whole novel.
Dickens gives him this lazy, drawling irony that functions as social armour — Eugene deflects everything with a kind of exquisite boredom.
He famously asks, when his friend Mortimer presses him about his intentions toward Lizzie Hexam, 'And so the force of will and purpose are strong in you, Mortimer?'
It is pure deflection — funny, elegant, and quite devastating as a portrait of a man who cannot yet commit to being himself.
Then the river nearly kills him, and that whole armour of irony is simply gone.
What he says to Lizzie from that near-death position is stripped bare — and you feel the enormous relief of it, as a reader and as a performer.
The Eugene Wrayburn arc is, I think, the most surprising thing in the novel — and I mean surprising in the very best sense.
Because Dickens sets him up as a type we might dismiss — the idle, well-born young man of the period.
And then he refuses to let us dismiss him.
When Eugene, lying broken after Headstone's murderous assault, summons the will to say that he wishes to be called Lizzie's husband — that is not satire.
That is Dickens the moralist insisting that even the most apparently hollow man contains the capacity for a genuine choice.
Burke would have understood it — the recovery of a man's better nature through suffering and love.
That is not a theme you arrive at through mere entertainment.
I think what Edmund is describing is real — but I want to defend the entertainment, because I think it's doing moral work too.
Take Mr. Venus — the articulator of human bones who sits in his dark shop surrounded by his specimens.
On the surface, he is pure comic grotesquery — one of the funniest inventions in all of Dickens.
But his melancholy — the rejected lover who keeps himself company with skeletons — carries a genuine pathos that the comedy doesn't cancel, it deepens.
When he eventually refuses to go on with Wegg's scheme against Boffin — when he withdraws on grounds of conscience — we believe it.
We believe it because Dickens has spent fifty pages making us fond of him through laughter.
The entertainment is the groundwork for the moral moment — not a separate operation at all.
Venus is one of the great Dickensian gifts — I will say that without any qualification whatsoever.
The scene where he explains to Wegg that he is 'not prepared to be regarded in the light of a friend' with all his characteristic mournful dignity — I could perform that all day.
But here is what I keep thinking about, regarding the entertainer-moralist question.
Dickens was doing the public readings in the last decade of his life — performing his own work, night after night, to enormous crowds.
He knew — he physically knew — when a crowd was with him, when the comedy landed, when the pathos hit.
And Our Mutual Friend, written in that same period, is saturated with that knowledge.
Dickens was not writing essays about society — he was engineering emotional events for an audience, in real time.
The moral argument arrives inside the experience — not before it, not after it.
I find myself, rather unexpectedly, agreeing with Oliver on that last point.
The moral argument arrives inside the experience — and nowhere in this novel is that more felt than in the treatment of the dust heaps themselves.
The great mounds of refuse from which Harmon's fortune was built are never explained as a symbol in the text.
Dickens simply presents them, looming over the story — and we feel their weight as moral fact, not as allegory.
That is artistry of a very high order — to make atmosphere do the work that rhetoric might otherwise bungle.
Johnson said that the only end of writing is to enable the reader better to enjoy life or better to endure it.
Our Mutual Friend, at its best, does both simultaneously — and that, I think, is the resolution of your entertainer-moralist tension.
What a way to put it — enjoy life and endure it, at the same time, on the same page.
We've been circling something important here — the way Dickens uses comic voice as moral instrument, whether it's Wegg's oily self-regard or Eugene's brittle irony or Venus's dignified grief.
In our next segment, we're going deeper into specific passages — the prose under the microscope.
Stay with us.

segments.title: The Weight of Gold: Social Critique and Individual Conscience

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
We've been exploring the novel's extraordinary richness — its grotesques, its river, its layered social world.
Now we turn to what may be Dickens's most sustained and searching theme in this book: the corrupting weight of money.
Our Mutual Friend is built on a dust heap — literally, a fortune made from sorting the refuse of London.
And from that foundation, Dickens asks: what does the anticipation of wealth do to a person's conscience, their relationships, their very sense of self?
Oliver, Edmund, Caroline — I'd like to start with the question of how Dickens frames money as a moral force from the very first pages.
What strikes me immediately — and it struck me on first reading and hasn't let go since — is how Dickens introduces money through absence and rumour.
John Harmon is dead before we properly meet him.
The Harmon fortune is a ghost haunting the living before any of them have touched a penny of it.
And then you get the Veneerings — ah, the Veneerings — who are money made flesh, money in evening dress, money sitting down to a dinner party.
Dickens gives us that magnificent phrase: 'bran-new people in a bran-new house in a bran-new quarter of London.'
'bran-new people in a bran-new house in a bran-new quarter of London.'
That triple repetition — it's a drumbeat of emptiness.
Everything new, nothing real, nothing earned.
Oliver is right to identify the Veneerings as central, but I'd resist the temptation to read them purely as satire of a class.
They are, rather, a study in the moral pathology of self-invention.
Dickens is asking a very old question — older than the novel form itself — which is: what happens to a man's character when his identity is purchased rather than formed?
Burke would have recognised it at once.

The Veneerings' magnificent table with its great looking-glass centrepiece — the guests see themselves reflected back, fragments of flattery and ambition — that is Dickens's image for a society that has lost the capacity for genuine self-knowledge.
Where there should be depth, there is only reflection.
What moves me about the novel's treatment of money is how intimate it is — how it gets inside the private relationships.
The Wilfer family — dear Rumty Wilfer and his terrifying wife — they live in a state of genteel, cheerful poverty, and Dickens renders that with such extraordinary tenderness.
And then Bella Wilfer is offered the Harmon fortune — offered, effectively, a life defined entirely by money — and her initial response is to want it.
She says — and this is Dickens at his most bracingly honest about human nature — that she is 'a mercenary little wretch.'
'a mercenary little wretch.'
She says it herself, about herself, with a kind of furious self-awareness that I find completely disarming.
It's not a flaw to be corrected from outside — it's a conscience already at work from within.
Caroline has put her finger on something crucial — Bella's arc is the novel's moral spine, really.
She's the character who most fully dramatises the question of whether a person can choose to be better than the world that shaped them.
And what Dickens understands — as a performer, I find this thrilling — is that the journey isn't from mercenary to saintly.
It's from self-knowledge to self-mastery.
The scene where she tends to her father — that little domestic idyll with Rumty — is where Dickens earns the emotional credibility for everything that follows.
I would go further and say that Bella Wilfer is one of the finest studies of individual conscience in all of Victorian fiction.
What distinguishes Dickens here — and I say this as someone not inclined to uncritical enthusiasm — is that he does not exempt her from the charge of worldliness.
He lets her be genuinely compromised by desire, by vanity, by the very reasonable human wish not to be poor.
And yet the transformation, when it comes, is earned — not by coincidence, not by inheritance restored, but by a private act of will.
She chooses John Rokesmith — the man she believes to be poor — with full knowledge of what she is surrendering.
That is moral seriousness of a high order.
But I want to press on the other side of the novel's social critique — the side that isn't about individual redemption but about structural cruelty.
Because Dickens gives us Eugene Wrayburn and Bradley Headstone — and that confrontation is not about conscience at all.
It's about class as a form of violence.
Headstone has clawed his way up through education — every penny of his learning is self-purchased — and Eugene dismisses him with the most devastating social contempt.
Eugene calls him 'the schoolmaster' — always 'the schoolmaster' — as though the category is sufficient to dispose of the man entirely.
And what breaks Headstone is not wickedness but thwarted dignity.
The Headstone-Wrayburn scenes are among the most electrically uncomfortable pages Dickens ever wrote.
Because we laugh with Eugene — he is genuinely witty, genuinely charming — and then we're made to feel the cost of that laughter.
There's a moment where Headstone confronts Eugene directly about Lizzie Hexam, and his passion comes out in these jagged, barely controlled sentences.
Dickens writes — and I read it as an actor who knows this rhythm — that Headstone 'spoke with his hands clenched and his teeth set.'
'spoke with his hands clenched and his teeth set.'
Five words of physical description and you know everything about a man imprisoned by his own body.
I'll concede that Headstone is brilliantly rendered — Dickens rarely draws a villain with such sympathy.
But I would caution against reading his fate as purely a social verdict.
Headstone's destruction comes ultimately from the choices he makes — the decision to stalk Eugene, to attempt murder, to submit to the blackmail of Rogue Riderhood.
Class may have shaped the pressures upon him, but character is what he does under pressure.
And in that final terrible scene at the lock — when he drags Riderhood into the river with him — we see not a victim of society but a man who has surrendered entirely to his worst self.
The social critique and the moral reckoning are inseparable in this novel.
That's the tension that makes the novel so alive, I think.
Dickens won't let you settle into either a purely social reading or a purely moral one.
And nowhere is that clearer than with old Mr. Boffin — the Golden Dustman — whose apparent transformation into a miser is the novel's great structural trick.
When Boffin begins to show an obsessive interest in misers — collecting books about them, quoting them at Bella with a kind of gleeful cruelty — it reads as genuinely disturbing.
Because Dickens has made us love Boffin — his goodness, his simplicity, his delight in Mrs. Boffin's 'wear.'
To watch him apparently corrupted by the Harmon gold is, in that middle section of the novel, genuinely heartbreaking.
The Boffin revelation is the moment I always want to talk about — because it divides readers completely.
When we learn that Boffin's miserliness has been a performance — an elaborate act staged to test and ultimately save Bella — some readers feel cheated.
And I understand that response.
But as a performer — someone who has spent his career inhabiting characters who perform for other characters — I find it magnificent.
Because the question it raises is profound: if you enact goodness, even deceptively, are you not still doing good?
Boffin plays a miser to cure Bella of mercenary desire — and it works.
The Boffin stratagem troubles me, I confess — not dramatically, but morally.
John Harmon — or Rokesmith, as we know him through most of the novel — has deceived Bella throughout their courtship.
He has tested the woman he loves as though she were a specimen under examination rather than a free moral agent.
Dickens gets away with it — just — because he has made us trust Harmon's fundamental decency.
But it is a reminder that even in this novel's most sympathetic characters, the desire to control — to arrange the moral outcomes of those one loves — is never entirely absent.
And perhaps that too is a form of the Harmon gold's corruption.
That's a remarkable note to pause on — the idea that even benevolent control carries the taint of the fortune that makes it possible.
The dust heap doesn't just make people wealthy — it makes them powerful over each other's lives.
We'll be returning, in our next segment, to the river — that other great symbolic force in the novel — and what it offers as an alternative to the world of gold.
Oliver, Edmund, Caroline — thank you.

segments.title: Closing: What Our Mutual Friend Owes Us

utterances.text: We've spent this episode deep inside Dickens's last completed novel — its river, its dust heaps, its resurrections.
But before we leave, I want to ask each of you a final question.
What does Our Mutual Friend owe us — and does it pay the debt?
It owes us a world — and by that I mean a fully inhabited, teeming, ridiculous, heartbreaking world.
And the extraordinary thing is that it delivers.
You have the Veneerings — that magnificent hollow couple hosting dinners for people who barely know them.
You have Silas Wegg and his wooden leg and his perfectly monstrous self-regard.
And then you have Jenny Wren — a child twisted by suffering who sees further than anyone.
That range — from Wegg's comic villainy to Jenny's visionary pain — that is what a great novelist owes you.
And Dickens pays it in full, with interest.
I would frame it differently — though I don't disagree with Oliver's relish.
What a novel of this ambition owes us is moral seriousness — the sense that character is being tested, and that the test matters.
And here Dickens delivers in ways that are sometimes underestimated.
Eugene Wrayburn's transformation is, I think, the novel's deepest achievement.
Here is a man of brilliant, dissipated intelligence who cannot find a reason to direct his gifts — until love and near-death force the question.
The novel asks whether a man like that can be saved — and it answers, quietly but firmly, yes.
That is not sentimentality. That is moral imagination at its most precise.
I keep coming back to what the novel owes its women — and whether it fully pays that particular debt.
Lizzie Hexam is one of the most purely good characters in all of Dickens — strong, steadfast, uncorrupted by the world around her.
And yet the novel's resolution essentially asks her to wait — to be rescued, to be married, to be completed by Eugene's reformation.
I feel the tension there. I always have, every re-reading.
But then I think of Bella Wilfer — and that is a different story altogether.
Bella begins the novel as frankly mercenary — she says so herself, with disarming honesty.
And her journey toward genuine feeling — fought for, not merely granted — is extraordinary.
So yes — the novel owes its women complexity. And it pays, unevenly but generously.
Caroline, I think you've put your finger on something that Dickens himself was negotiating in real time.
This is a late novel — written by a man who had seen the world, lost his illusions, and kept his comedy.
There's a line Jenny Wren delivers — about her drunken father — that I think captures the whole spirit of the book.
She says to him — her own father, mind you — 'You are not my child.'
It's the world turned upside down — the child parenting the parent, the innocent judging the guilty.
And Dickens delivers that inversion with no fuss — just the bare, devastating line.
That is what great performance writing looks like on the page.
I should like to add one thing about the dust heaps — since we have circled around them all episode.
One occasionally hears that they are a symbol — of capitalism, of waste, of some grand systemic indictment.
I am more persuaded that they are simply what Dickens always sought — a concrete, vivid, slightly absurd thing that carries enormous weight.
Old Harmon's fortune built from rubbish — that is not a treatise on political economy.
That is the ancient story of inheritance, corruption, and the difficulty of beginning afresh.
John Harmon's disguise, his long circuit back to himself — that is what the novel is really about.
Not systems. Souls.
Edmund says 'not systems, souls' — and I think that's beautifully put, even if I'd resist the strict either-or.
Because the genius of the novel is that the souls are shaped by the systems — you can't fully separate them.
Rogue Riderhood, Bradley Headstone — these men are destroyed by forces partly inside and partly outside themselves.
That is the thing that stays with me on every re-reading.
The novel refuses easy consolation — even its happy endings carry a kind of shadow.
Boffin turns out to have been good all along — but the reader was fooled, and that fooling was deliberate.
We were made to feel the pull of money, of corruption, of watching a good man turn.
That is what the novel owes us — and delivers: the experience, not just the moral.
Systems and souls — and the river running through both.
Oliver, Edmund, Caroline — you've made me want to start reading from page one all over again. Which is, I think, the highest possible compliment.
Our Mutual Friend is a novel that asks a great deal of its reader — in length, in darkness, in complexity.
And as our guests have shown today, it gives back even more.
Thank you for joining us on Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
Until next time — keep reading, keep listening, and keep the river in mind.

c24:p88.text:
Mr Wegg then goes on to enlarge upon what throughout has been uppermost in
      his crafty mind:—the qualifications of Mr Venus for such a search.
      He expatiates on Mr Venus’s patient habits and delicate manipulation; on
      his skill in piecing little things together; on his knowledge of various
      tissues and textures; on the likelihood of small indications leading him
      on to the discovery of great concealments. ‘While as to myself,’ says
      Wegg, ‘I am not good at it. Whether I gave myself up to prodding, or
      whether I gave myself up to scooping, I couldn’t do it with that delicate
      touch so as not to show that I was disturbing the mounds. Quite different
      with  you , going to work (as  you  would) in the light of a fellow-man,
      holily pledged in a friendly move to his brother man.’ Mr Wegg next
      modestly remarks on the want of adaptation in a wooden leg to ladders and
      such like airy perches, and also hints at an inherent tendency in that
      timber fiction, when called into action for the purposes of a promenade on
      an ashey slope, to stick itself into the yielding foothold, and peg its
      owner to one spot. Then, leaving this part of the subject, he remarks on
      the special phenomenon that before his installation in the Bower, it was
      from Mr Venus that he first heard of the legend of hidden wealth in the
      Mounds: ‘which’, he observes with a vaguely pious air, ‘was surely never
      meant for nothing.’ Lastly, he returns to the cause of the right, gloomily
      foreshadowing the possibility of something being unearthed to criminate Mr
      Boffin (of whom he once more candidly admits it cannot be denied that he
      profits by a murder), and anticipating his denunciation by the friendly
      movers to avenging justice. And this, Mr Wegg expressly points out, not at
      all for the sake of the reward—though it would be a want of
      principle not to take it.
c24:p88.summary: Wegg elaborates on Venus's qualifications for the search—his patience, delicate touch, skill at reconstruction—while admitting his own limitations and hinting at Boffin's culpability.

c63:p15.text:
‘Harkee to me, deary,’ pursued Mrs Boffin, taking Bella’s hands between
      her own, and gently beating on them from time to time. ‘It was after a
      particular night when John had been disappointed—as he thought—in
      his affections. It was after a night when John had made an offer to a
      certain young lady, and the certain young lady had refused it. It was
      after a particular night, when he felt himself cast-away-like, and had
      made up his mind to go seek his fortune. It was the very next night. My
      Noddy wanted a paper out of his Secretary’s room, and I says to Noddy, “I
      am going by the door, and I’ll ask him for it.” I tapped at his door, and
      he didn’t hear me. I looked in, and saw him a sitting lonely by his fire,
      brooding over it. He chanced to look up with a pleased kind of smile in my
      company when he saw me, and then in a single moment every grain of the
      gunpowder that had been lying sprinkled thick about him ever since I first
      set eyes upon him as a man at the Bower, took fire! Too many a time had I
      seen him sitting lonely, when he was a poor child, to be pitied, heart and
      hand! Too many a time had I seen him in need of being brightened up with a
      comforting word! Too many and too many a time to be mistaken, when that
      glimpse of him come at last! No, no! I just makes out to cry, “I know you
      now! You’re John!” And he catches me as I drops.—So what,’ says Mrs
      Boffin, breaking off in the rush of her speech to smile most radiantly,
      ‘might you think by this time that your husband’s name was, dear?’
c63:p15.summary: Mrs Boffin reveals how she discovered John's true identity when she found him brooding by his fire; her recognition was triggered by memories of him as a poor child at the Bower, and the emotional moment caused her to cry out his name.
c63:p15.best_quote: Too many a time had I seen him sitting lonely, when he was a poor child, to be pitied, heart and hand! Too many a time had I seen him in need of being brightened up with a comforting word!

c20:p51.text:
‘My love,’ says Lady Tippins, ‘compose yourself; we’ll bring him in.’ And
      Lady Tippins really does work, and work the Veneering horses too; for she
      clatters about town all day, calling upon everybody she knows, and showing
      her entertaining powers and green fan to immense advantage, by rattling on
      with, My dear soul, what do you think? What do you suppose me to be?
      You’ll never guess. I’m pretending to be an electioneering agent. And for
      what place of all places? Pocket-Breaches. And why? Because the dearest
      friend I have in the world has bought it. And who is the dearest friend I
      have in the world? A man of the name of Veneering. Not omitting his wife,
      who is the other dearest friend I have in the world; and I positively
      declare I forgot their baby, who is the other. And we are carrying on this
      little farce to keep up appearances, and isn’t it refreshing! Then, my
      precious child, the fun of it is that nobody knows who these Veneerings
      are, and that they know nobody, and that they have a house out of the
      Tales of the Genii, and give dinners out of the Arabian Nights. Curious to
      see ’em, my dear? Say you’ll know ’em. Come and dine with ’em. They shan’t
      bore you. Say who shall meet you. We’ll make up a party of our own, and
      I’ll engage that they shall not interfere with you for one single moment.
      You really ought to see their gold and silver camels. I call their
      dinner-table, the Caravan. Do come and dine with my Veneerings, my own
      Veneerings, my exclusive property, the dearest friends I have in the
      world! And above all, my dear, be sure you promise me your vote and
      interest and all sorts of plumpers for Pocket-Breaches; for we couldn’t
      think of spending sixpence on it, my love, and can only consent to be
      brought in by the spontaneous thingummies of the incorruptible
      whatdoyoucallums.
c20:p51.summary: Lady Tippins enthusiastically spreads the word about Veneering's candidacy, revealing her cynical view that the whole enterprise is a theatrical farce designed to keep up appearances, while openly admitting the Veneerings are unknowns with a spectacular house and ridiculous dinners.

      his breast, looked at him lying with his right hand clenched in his sleep
      and his teeth set, until a film came over his own sight, and he slept too.
      He awoke to find that it was daylight, and that his visitor was already
      astir, and going out to the river-side to cool his head:—‘Though I’m
      blest,’ muttered Riderhood at the Lock-house door, looking after him, ‘if
      I think there’s water enough in all the Thames to do  that  for you!’ Within
      five minutes he had taken his departure, and was passing on into the calm
      distance as he had passed yesterday. Riderhood knew when a fish leaped, by

The great looking-glass above the sideboard, reflects the table and the
      company. Reflects the new Veneering crest, in gold and eke in silver,
      frosted and also thawed, a camel of all work. The Heralds’ College found
      out a Crusading ancestor for Veneering who bore a camel on his shield (or
      might have done it if he had thought of it), and a caravan of camels take
      charge of the fruits and flowers and candles, and kneel down to be loaded
      with the salt. Reflects Veneering; forty, wavy-haired, dark, tending to
      corpulence, sly, mysterious, filmy—a kind of sufficiently
      well-looking veiled-prophet, not prophesying. Reflects Mrs Veneering;
      fair, aquiline-nosed and fingered, not so much light hair as she might
      have, gorgeous in raiment and jewels, enthusiastic, propitiatory,
      conscious that a corner of her husband’s veil is over herself. Reflects
      Podsnap; prosperously feeding, two little light-coloured wiry wings, one
      on either side of his else bald head, looking as like his hairbrushes as
      his hair, dissolving view of red beads on his forehead, large allowance of
      crumpled shirt-collar up behind. Reflects Mrs Podsnap; fine woman for
      Professor Owen, quantity of bone, neck and nostrils like a rocking-horse,
      hard features, majestic head-dress in which Podsnap has hung golden
      offerings. Reflects Twemlow; grey, dry, polite, susceptible to east wind,
      First-Gentleman-in-Europe collar and cravat, cheeks drawn in as if he had
      made a great effort to retire into himself some years ago, and had got so
      far and had never got any farther. Reflects mature young lady; raven
      locks, and complexion that lights up well when well powdered—as it
      is—carrying on considerably in the captivation of mature young
      gentleman; with too much nose in his face, too much ginger in his
      whiskers, too much torso in his waistcoat, too much sparkle in his studs,
      his eyes, his buttons, his talk, and his teeth. Reflects charming old Lady
      Tippins on Veneering’s right; with an immense obtuse drab oblong face,
      like a face in a tablespoon, and a dyed Long Walk up the top of her head,
      as a convenient public approach to the bunch of false hair behind, pleased
      to patronize Mrs Veneering opposite, who is pleased to be patronized.
      Reflects a certain ‘Mortimer’, another of Veneering’s oldest friends; who
      never was in the house before, and appears not to want to come again, who
      sits disconsolate on Mrs Veneering’s left, and who was inveigled by Lady
      Tippins (a friend of his boyhood) to come to these people’s and talk, and
      who won’t talk. Reflects Eugene, friend of Mortimer; buried alive in the
      back of his chair, behind a shoulder—with a powder-epaulette on it—of
      the mature young lady, and gloomily resorting to the champagne chalice
      whenever proffered by the Analytical Chemist. Lastly, the looking-glass
      reflects Boots and Brewer, and two other stuffed Buffers interposed
      between the rest of the company and possible accidents.
c2:p24.summary: The looking-glass above the sideboard reflects the assembled guests, with Dickens offering detailed satirical physical and character descriptions of each person.

c67:p57.text:
When I devised this story, I foresaw the likelihood that a class of
      readers and commentators would suppose that I was at great pains to
      conceal exactly what I was at great pains to suggest: namely, that Mr John
      Harmon was not slain, and that Mr John Rokesmith was he. Pleasing myself
      with the idea that the supposition might in part arise out of some
      ingenuity in the story, and thinking it worth while, in the interests of
      art, to hint to an audience that an artist (of whatever denomination) may
      perhaps be trusted to know what he is about in his vocation, if they will
      concede him a little patience, I was not alarmed by the anticipation.
c67:p57.summary: Dickens explains that he intentionally created ambiguity about John Harmon's identity and asks readers to trust his artistic judgment and patience with the serialized format.
c67:p57.best_quote: I foresaw the likelihood that a class of readers and commentators would suppose that I was at great pains to conceal exactly what I was at great pains to suggest: namely, that Mr John Harmon was not slain, and that Mr John Rokesmith was he.

c2:p3.text:
But, it was not this which steeped the feeble soul of Twemlow in
      confusion. This he was used to, and could take soundings of. The abyss to
      which he could find no bottom, and from which started forth the engrossing
      and ever-swelling difficulty of his life, was the insoluble question
      whether he was Veneering’s oldest friend, or newest friend. To the
      excogitation of this problem, the harmless gentleman had devoted many
      anxious hours, both in his lodgings over the livery stable-yard, and in
      the cold gloom, favourable to meditation, of Saint James’s Square. Thus.
      Twemlow had first known Veneering at his club, where Veneering then knew
      nobody but the man who made them known to one another, who seemed to be
      the most intimate friend he had in the world, and whom he had known two
      days—the bond of union between their souls, the nefarious conduct of
      the committee respecting the cookery of a fillet of veal, having been
      accidentally cemented at that date. Immediately upon this, Twemlow
      received an invitation to dine with Veneering, and dined: the man being of
      the party. Immediately upon that, Twemlow received an invitation to dine
      with the man, and dined: Veneering being of the party. At the man’s were a
      Member, an Engineer, a Payer-off of the National Debt, a Poem on
      Shakespeare, a Grievance, and a Public Office, who all seem to be utter
      strangers to Veneering. And yet immediately after that, Twemlow received
      an invitation to dine at Veneerings, expressly to meet the Member, the
      Engineer, the Payer-off of the National Debt, the Poem on Shakespeare, the
      Grievance, and the Public Office, and, dining, discovered that all of them
      were the most intimate friends Veneering had in the world, and that the
      wives of all of them (who were all there) were the objects of Mrs
      Veneering’s most devoted affection and tender confidence.
c2:p3.summary: Twemlow recounts his baffling experience of being introduced to Veneering, noting how Veneering's friends constantly shift and how he cannot determine his own position in the social hierarchy.
c2:p3.best_quote: the insoluble question whether he was Veneering's oldest friend, or newest friend

c20:p32.text:
Meanwhile Twemlow, in an increasing hurry of spirits, gets his hair down
      as well as he can—which is not very well; for, after these glutinous
      applications it is restive, and has a surface on it somewhat in the nature
      of pastry—and gets to the club by the appointed time. At the club he
      promptly secures a large window, writing materials, and all the
      newspapers, and establishes himself; immoveable, to be respectfully
      contemplated by Pall Mall. Sometimes, when a man enters who nods to him,
      Twemlow says, ‘Do you know Veneering?’ Man says, ‘No; member of the club?’
      Twemlow says, ‘Yes. Coming in for Pocket-Breaches.’ Man says, ‘Ah! Hope he
      may find it worth the money!’ yawns, and saunters out. Towards six o’clock
      of the afternoon, Twemlow begins to persuade himself that he is positively
      jaded with work, and thinks it much to be regretted that he was not
      brought up as a Parliamentary agent.
c20:p32.summary: Twemlow settles at his club with window seat, writing materials, and newspapers; he engages in the absurdist 'work' of telling men about Veneering, eventually convincing himself he is exhausted by labour.
c20:p32.best_quote: Towards six o'clock of the afternoon, Twemlow begins to persuade himself that he is positively jaded with work, and thinks it much to be regretted that he was not brought up as a Parliamentary agent

c67:p58.text:
To keep for a long time unsuspected, yet always working itself out,
      another purpose originating in that leading incident, and turning it to a
      pleasant and useful account at last, was at once the most interesting and
      the most difficult part of my design. Its difficulty was much enhanced by
      the mode of publication; for, it would be very unreasonable to expect that
      many readers, pursuing a story in portions from month to month through
      nineteen months, will, until they have it before them complete, perceive
      the relations of its finer threads to the whole pattern which is always
      before the eyes of the story-weaver at his loom. Yet, that I hold the
      advantages of the mode of publication to outweigh its disadvantages, may
      be easily believed of one who revived it in the Pickwick Papers after long
      disuse, and has pursued it ever since.
c67:p58.summary: Dickens reflects on the difficulty of maintaining a secret subplot across serialized publication, defending the mode of publication despite its challenges.
c67:p58.best_quote: To keep for a long time unsuspected, yet always working itself out, another purpose originating in that leading incident, and turning it to a pleasant and useful account at last, was at once the most interesting and the most difficult part of my design.

c67:p60.text:
In my social experiences since Mrs Betty Higden came upon the scene and
      left it, I have found Circumlocutional champions disposed to be warm with
      me on the subject of my view of the Poor Law. My friend Mr Bounderby could
      never see any difference between leaving the Coketown ‘hands’ exactly as
      they were, and requiring them to be fed with turtle soup and venison out
      of gold spoons. Idiotic propositions of a parallel nature have been freely
      offered for my acceptance, and I have been called upon to admit that I
      would give Poor Law relief to anybody, anywhere, anyhow. Putting this
      nonsense aside, I have observed a suspicious tendency in the champions to
      divide into two parties; the one, contending that there are no deserving
      Poor who prefer death by slow starvation and bitter weather, to the
      mercies of some Relieving Officers and some Union Houses; the other,
      admitting that there are such Poor, but denying that they have any cause
      or reason for what they do. The records in our newspapers, the late
      exposure by  The Lancet , and the common sense and senses of common people,
      furnish too abundant evidence against both defences. But, that my view of
      the Poor Law may not be mistaken or misrepresented, I will state it. I
      believe there has been in England, since the days of the  Stuarts , no law
      so often infamously administered, no law so often openly violated, no law
      habitually so ill-supervised. In the majority of the shameful cases of
      disease and death from destitution, that shock the Public and disgrace the
      country, the illegality is quite equal to the inhumanity—and known
      language could say no more of their lawlessness.
c67:p60.summary: Dickens defends his critique of the Poor Law as grounded in observable fact and ethical principle, arguing it is the most infamously administered law in English history.
c67:p60.best_quote: I believe there has been in England, since the days of the Stuarts, no law so often infamously administered, no law so often openly violated, no law habitually so ill-supervised. In the majority of the shameful cases of disease and death from destitution, that shock the Public and disgrace the country, the illegality is quite equal to the inhumanity—and known language could say no more of their lawlessness.

c67:p21.text:
‘Hardly so, I think,’ the stubborn Mortimer strikes in. ‘I take the
      question to be, whether such a man as you describe, Lady Tippins, does
      right or wrong in marrying a brave woman (I say nothing of her beauty),
      who has saved his life, with a wonderful energy and address; whom he knows
      to be virtuous, and possessed of remarkable qualities; whom he has long
      admired, and who is deeply attached to him.’
c67:p21.summary: Mortimer forcefully reframes the question, arguing that marrying a virtuous, brave woman of remarkable qualities makes Eugene a greater gentleman, not a fool.
c67:p21.best_quote: I take the question to be, whether such a man as you describe, Lady Tippins, does right or wrong in marrying a brave woman (I say nothing of her beauty), who has saved his life, with a wonderful energy and address; whom he knows to be virtuous, and possessed of remarkable qualities; whom he has long admired, and who is deeply attached to him.

c2:p85.text:
‘Why, no,’ says Mortimer; ‘remarkable thing, you are all wrong. The story
      is completer and rather more exciting than I supposed. Man’s drowned!’
c2:p85.summary: Mortimer delivers the shocking news that John Harmon has drowned, completely overturning expectations and creating the novel's central mystery.

c33:p39.text:
‘The reference,’ proceeds Mortimer, ‘which I suppose to be made by my
      honourable and fair enslaver opposite, is to the following circumstance.
      Very lately, the young woman, Lizzie Hexam, daughter of the late Jesse
      Hexam, otherwise Gaffer, who will be remembered to have found the body of
      the man from somewhere, mysteriously received, she knew not from whom, an
      explicit retraction of the charges made against her father, by another
      water-side character of the name of Riderhood. Nobody believed them,
      because little Rogue Riderhood—I am tempted into the paraphrase by
      remembering the charming wolf who would have rendered society a great
      service if he had devoured Mr Riderhood’s father and mother in their
      infancy—had previously played fast and loose with the said charges,
      and, in fact, abandoned them. However, the retraction I have mentioned
      found its way into Lizzie Hexam’s hands, with a general flavour on it of
      having been favoured by some anonymous messenger in a dark cloak and
      slouched hat, and was by her forwarded, in her father’s vindication, to Mr
      Boffin, my client. You will excuse the phraseology of the shop, but as I
      never had another client, and in all likelihood never shall have, I am
      rather proud of him as a natural curiosity probably unique.’
c33:p39.summary: Mortimer recounts how Lizzie Hexam mysteriously received a retraction of charges against her father from Riderhood, which she forwarded to Boffin in vindication, establishing the foundation for her subsequent disappearance.
c33:p39.best_quote: little Rogue Riderhood—I am tempted into the paraphrase by remembering the charming wolf who would have rendered society a great service if he had devoured Mr Riderhood's father and mother in their infancy

c67:p61.text:
On Friday the Ninth of June in the present year, Mr and Mrs Boffin (in
      their manuscript dress of receiving Mr and Mrs Lammle at breakfast) were
      on the South Eastern Railway with me, in a terribly destructive accident.
      When I had done what I could to help others, I climbed back into my
      carriage—nearly turned over a viaduct, and caught aslant upon the
      turn—to extricate the worthy couple. They were much soiled, but
      otherwise unhurt. The same happy result attended Miss Bella Wilfer on her
      wedding day, and Mr Riderhood inspecting Bradley Headstone’s red
      neckerchief as he lay asleep. I remember with devout thankfulness that I
      can never be much nearer parting company with my readers for ever, than I
      was then, until there shall be written against my life, the two words with
      which I have this day closed this book:—THE END.
c67:p61.summary: Dickens recounts his experience in the Staplehurst railway accident of June 9, 1865, expressing gratitude for his miraculous escape and reflecting on mortality in connection with the novel's conclusion.
c67:p61.best_quote: I remember with devout thankfulness that I can never be much nearer parting company with my readers for ever, than I was then, until there shall be written against my life, the two words with which I have this day closed this book:—THE END.
